title: The cantonists
hook: Jewish boys are conscripted into the Russian army for a lifetime of service

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Pale: a line in law that a trader could not ride past. Your line was a fence kept around you. Where did you go freely? Today, the hardest thing the empire took from inside that line. Day nine hundred sixty-nine.

Some songs are sung so a child will fall asleep. Others are sung so a child will be remembered. In the Yiddish-speaking towns of the Russian Empire, there were songs of the second kind: about a boy snatched from his bed at night, about a mother running after a wagon, about men who came for the children of the poor. These are not fairy tales. They are memories set to a tune, about a real law and real boys. Today, the cantonists. A gentle warning: this one is about children taken from their families.
screen: `SONGS SO A CHILD WILL BE REMEMBERED.` → `A BOY SNATCHED AT NIGHT.` → `A REAL LAW, REAL BOYS.`

segments.voice: Under Tsar Nicholas the First, the Russian Empire began drafting Jews into its army, and it did something especially cruel with Jewish boys. Boys who were not yet old enough to be soldiers could be taken anyway and sent to military schools for soldiers' children, called cantonist schools, often very far from home. The army service that followed was so long that a boy taken as a child might come home a grown man, if he came home at all. In those schools, the boys were pressed, sometimes brutally, to be baptized and leave Judaism behind. Some held on. Some could not. And there is a part of this story that is painful to tell, and is told honestly in Jewish memory. The empire made each Jewish community responsible for handing over its own quota of recruits. So the choosing fell on the community's leaders. Too often, the sons of the poor and the orphans were the ones handed over, and men called khappers, snatchers, were hired to seize boys when families hid them. The wound ran outward, against the empire, and inward too. The prophet Jeremiah gave this kind of grief its words: "A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not." Rachel, the matriarch, weeping for children who are gone. And the next verse answers her: "they shall come again from the land of the enemy." Some of the cantonists did come back. Some had kept their faith in secret all those years. Their stories, and the songs about them, are how a people refused to let those boys be forgotten.
screen: `BOYS TAKEN TO CANTONIST SCHOOLS.` · `PRESSED TO LEAVE JUDAISM.` · `A QUOTA THE COMMUNITY HAD TO FILL.` · `RACHEL WEEPING FOR HER CHILDREN.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL COME AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: remember children taken. Sit still, and let your breath be slow and quiet. Bring to mind one boy from this story. You don't know his name, and that's all right. He might be very young. Let him be real for a moment: a bed, a mother, a town he could not return to. Then widen your attention to children today who are taken from their families, by war, by law, by people who should have protected them. You don't need to fix anything in these two minutes. Just refuse, for this moment, to forget them. If you pray, you can hold them there. The bell holds the time.
The cantonists. Jewish boys taken into the Russian army as children, sent to schools far from home and pressed to give up their faith. Today's word.
Your line: the taken children. Today, say one of their stories out loud to someone, or simply speak the words the cantonists, so the memory travels one more step. Day nine hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: The cantonists are remembered in Yiddish songs, memoirs and later histories, and some Jewish families still tell stories of ancestors who were taken or who hid their sons.
